Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in an interview with Al Jazeera that Tehran has no desire to continue the war with the US, but that the ball is in Washington’s court for peace talks.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?
Saudi Arabia is believed to be expanding its Chinese-designed ballistic missile arsenal as it faces an unprecedented barrage of missile and drone attacks from Yemen's Houthi forces.
Satellite imagery analysed by American researchers suggests the kingdom is expanding its ballistic missile plant at al-Duwadimi in Riyadh Province to build larger solid-fuel missiles capable of carrying heavier payloads across greater distances.
Fighting between the kingdom and the Iran-aligned Yemeni group has intensified since July, shattering a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.
The Houthis have stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi cities, airports and energy infrastructure, retaliating for what they call a Saudi "blockade" of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
Analysts have told Middle East Eye that the renewed confrontation with the Houthis has given the kingdom's arsenal added significance.

An Israeli soldier takes position at a checkpoint in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on 23 October 2026 (Ahmad Gharabali/AFP)

Several Israeli firms whose military equipment has been used in the genocidal war on Gaza are heading to India later this month to explore partnerships with local firms, Middle East Eye can reveal.
Twenty Israeli companies are expected to attend a start-up event in Hyderabad, Telangana, on 16 November, organised by T-Hub, which describes itself as "the world's largest startup hub", supporting founders through programmes, partnerships and access to global markets.
A further 25 Israeli companies are expected at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, billed as Asia's premier platform for technology, commerce and innovation, which runs from 17 to 19 November.
The companies include XTEND, whose drones have been deployed by Israeli forces in Gaza, including one allegedly used to track and film the killing of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar on 16 October 2024.
Also attending are Dagan-Optics, a supplier of equipment to Israeli military units, and Netzer Precision, whose sensors are incorporated into Israeli tanks and armoured personnel carriers.
The summits are intended to provide opportunities for technological collaboration and commercial partnerships between Israeli tech companies and local firms.
An MEE analysis of the companies scheduled to attend has found that several are either directly involved in Israel's military operations in Gaza or materially connected to the country's wider military-industrial complex, including its occupation infrastructure in the occupied West Bank.

data.title: Middle East Eye: How Israel's war on Lebanon's water has become existential
data.author: Zaynab Mayladan
data.summary:
How Israel's war on Lebanon's water has become existential
Submitted by
Zaynab Mayladan
on
Mon, 11/02/2026 - 19:08
Across the country's south, where water infrastructure has been targeted for decades, the ongoing conflict raises a key question: can life here ever get back to normal?
Insaf Faour and her granddaughter, Fatima, are pictured in August 2026 at their home in Debaal, Lebanon, which has been hit hard in Israel’s war (MEE/Zaynab Mayladan)
Off
It was half past five in the afternoon when Bahij Abdallah saw a white object pass overhead.
He was outside a pumping station in Ebel el-Saqi, in the hills above Marjayoun, checking on an open water reservoir. He had sat down on a stone step with his phone in his hand, while three colleagues remained inside.
At first, he thought the white thing was a drone.
“Suddenly, it stopped in the air for a second, turned, and fell on the station,” Abdallah told Middle East Eye. “Then the smoke and the fire started.”
The phone flew out of his hand. He felt a wall of air, and then metal pushing into his body. He looked down and saw blood dripping from his face. His shoulder was burning. When he stood up, he saw that his shoe had been cut open.
Abdallah, an electrical maintenance employee with the South Lebanon Water Establishment (SLWE), the state utility that supplies drinking water to two governorates, had been doing what he does most days: running the station and monitoring it.
The facility is well known in the region and clearly marked, he said. “There are signs, and vehicles with the name and logo on them, that it belongs to the South Lebanon Water Establishment, which is a government body. And we were wearing the work uniform.”
The attack occurred on 9 June 2026, five days after Israel and the Lebanese government announced in Washington that they had agreed to a ceasefire.
'I could have died in seconds. And I wasn't doing anything wrong; I was only pumping water for people to drink'
- Bahij Abdallah, state utility worker

An image of a Toyota forklift at a missiles and ammunition centre in northern Israel, as posted on Israeli military social media accounts on 7 July. (Facebook)

Toyota has said it is investigating the use of its forklifts by the Israeli military after Middle East Eye found photos and videos of the vehicles at weapons and munitions storage sites, serving supply lines for frontline units, and being used by the army’s Logistics Corps.
It comes after MEE uncovered details of a previously unreported 158m-shekel ($49.8m) contract between Toyota and Israel’s Ministry of Defense for the supply of forklifts that was signed in 2024 – the first full year of the Gaza war.
Toyota says that its vehicles are not intended for military use.
When asked about the contract, the company told MEE it had commitments in place with both the defence ministry and its official reseller in Israel to ensure that its technology and products were “for civil use only”.
But when MEE then shared footage posted on official Israeli military social media channels, which showed Toyota forklifts being used at locations including a missiles and ammunition depot in northern Israel, a Logistics Corps training base, and inside a munitions factory, it said it was investigating the images to determine whether those agreements had been breached.
Toyota is a Japanese corporation but its main forklift business, Toyota Material Handling, is headquartered in the United States.

data.author: Mee User
data.summary:
India clears Israeli firm Cellebrite to supply phone-hacking tools to government agencies
India has exempted Israeli surveillance company Cellebrite from domestic procurement rules, allowing government agencies to purchase its phone-extraction and hacking technology, an investigation has found.
The digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found that Home Minister Amit Shah approved a waiver for the National Investigation Agency (NIA), clearing the way for the purchase of at least 422 foreign forensic products, including Cellebrite tools.
The technology can extract data from seized devices and use recovered login tokens to access more than 100 cloud services, including social media platforms such as Instagram, X and Tinder.
Digital-rights experts have warned that the expansion of surveillance capabilities raises serious privacy concerns, with India's existing laws offering inadequate safeguards against excessive monitoring.

data.title: Middle East Eye: French government condemns Israel entry ban on Jean-Luc Melenchon
data.author: Alex MacDonald
data.summary:
French government condemns Israel entry ban on Jean-Luc Melenchon
Submitted by
Alex MacDonald
on
Fri, 11/13/2026 - 09:34
Foreign minister accuses Netanyahu of 'demagogic' move after ban announced on left-wing presidential contender
La France Insoumise presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon attends a ceremony dedicated to victims of WWI, in Gentioux-Pigerolles, central France, on 11 November 2026 (Pascal Lachenaud/AFP)
Off
The French government has condemned Israel for blocking left-wing political leader and presidential contender Jean-Luc Melenchon from the country.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot described the move as a "demagogic decision" by the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, which he said "has repeatedly violated international law".
Barrot, an opponent of Melenchon and his La France Insoumise (LFI) party, said Israel's move “plays into the hands of those who, like La France Insoumise, live off the instrumentalisation of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict”.
The ban on Melenchon was announced on Thursday, citing the veteran politician's criticism of Israel's occupation and genocide in Gaza.
Israeli Interior Minister Gideon Sa’ar accused Melenchon of "blood libels" against Israel, specifically citing his promise last week to send ships to accompany Gaza aid flotillas if elected president.
It also comes a week after France refused admission to the country to Israeli settler Yossi Dagan, head of the Samaria Regional Council in the northern occupied West Bank.
France is set for elections in 2027 that could see the far-right National Rally win the presidency for the first time. Its leader Marine Le Pen is leading in polls, with Melenchon her nearest rival.

Hospitals, schools and residential buildings have been bombed. Water and sanitation infrastructure have been destroyed, amid warnings of mass malnutrition and starvation.
No, these are not headlines from Gaza - although they could be. They are from Iran and Lebanon, two countries that have been systematically targeted by the Israeli military over the past three years.
Yet the destruction of civilian life in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran is not an isolated phenomenon. Across different political contexts, Muslim and Muslim-adjacent populations have long been subjected to violence, abandonment and containment.
Well before 2023, hundreds of civilians were killed by US drone warfare in Yemen; refugees attempting to reach Europe were abandoned to death in the Mediterranean by the EU; and millions of displaced Syrians were warehoused in camps enclosed with barbed wire.
What connects these, and countless other cases, is the discourse of terrorism. It does not simply identify populations as security threats; it justifies managing those threats through lethal means. Death is administered immediately or slowly, by creating conditions that expose people to premature death.
These interconnected practices of death-dealing across multiple geographical sites reveal the global operations of anti-Muslim racism.

data.author: Mee User
data.summary:
Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
Toyota has said it is investigating the use of its forklifts by the Israeli military after Middle East Eye found photos and videos of the vehicles at weapons and munitions storage sites, serving supply lines for frontline units, and being used by the army’s Logistics Corps.
It comes after MEE uncovered details of a previously unreported 158m-shekel ($49.8m) contract between Toyota and Israel’s Ministry of Defense for the supply of forklifts that was signed in 2024 – the first full year of the Gaza war.
Toyota says that its vehicles are not intended for military use.
When asked about the contract, the company told MEE it had commitments in place with both the defence ministry and its official reseller in Israel to ensure that its technology and products were “for civil use only”.
But when MEE then shared footage posted on official Israeli military social media channels, which showed Toyota forklifts being used at locations including a missiles and ammunition depot in northern Israel, a Logistics Corps training base, and inside a munitions factory, it said it was investigating the images to determine whether those agreements had been breached.

data.author: Mee User

Iran reports shooting down US Predator drone off its southern coast
Iran’s navy said on Friday that it shot down a US MQ-1 Predator drone over the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media.
The semi-official IRNA news agency reported that the drone was downed near the Sirik coast in the Kuhestak region.
The navy said it “will not hesitate for a moment” to defend Iran’s territorial integrity, maritime borders and interests.
Images shared by IRNA appear to show damaged components of military hardware.
